lessons.title: Making plans

tip.title: Suggesting with on
tip.body: In everyday French, on usually means 'we': On se retrouve où ? (where shall we meet?). To suggest something, use On pourrait + infinitive (we could …) or, with friends, Ça te dit de + infinitive ? (do you fancy …?). For plans that depend on something, use si + present: S'il fait beau, on ira au parc. si becomes s' only before il and ils. Pronunciation: on_ira has a liaison — 'on-ni-ra'.

lessons.title: Accepting and declining
lessons.goal: Invite someone, accept or decline an invitation and give a reason.

tip.title: Yes, no and why
tip.body: To accept: Avec plaisir ! or Volontiers ! (gladly). To decline politely, apologise and give a reason with parce que or just a comma: Désolé, je ne peux pas, je dois travailler. Women write désolée — it sounds the same. In speech the ne often disappears: J'peux pas. In volontiers the final rs is silent: 'vo-lon-tyé'.

lessons.title: Planning a trip
lessons.goal: Talk about where, how and how long you will travel.

tip.title: huit jours, quinze jours
tip.body: French people often say huit jours for a week and quinze jours for two weeks — it counts both end days. partir means to leave or go away (Cet été, on part en Bretagne), rester means to stay, not 'to rest'. y replaces a place already mentioned: On y va en train ? (Shall we go there by train?). Pronunciation: the t of huit is silent before a consonant (huit jours = 'ui jour') but heard before a vowel (huit heures).

lessons.title: The simple future
lessons.goal: Use the futur simple for plans, predictions and promises.

tip.title: Infinitive + -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont
tip.body: Take the infinitive and add the endings: je parlerai, tu parleras, il parlera, nous parlerons, vous parlerez, ils parleront. -re verbs drop the final e: prendre → je prendrai. Some key verbs have an irregular stem: être → je serai, avoir → j'aurai, aller → j'irai, faire → je ferai, venir → je viendrai, pouvoir → je pourrai, voir → je verrai. Every stem ends in r. Use the futur proche (je vais partir) for near, certain plans and the futur simple for further plans, predictions and promises. Unlike English, French uses the future after quand: Quand j'aurai le temps … . Si + present → future: S'il pleut, je resterai à la maison. Pronunciation: the je ending -ai sounds like 'é', and the e in parlerai is often swallowed: 'parl'ré'.

lessons.title: Your next holiday
lessons.goal: Talk about your plans for 40 seconds.

culture.title: Juillet, août and la rentrée
culture.body: Many people in France take their main holiday in July or August, often two or three weeks in a row. People joke about juillettistes (July holidaymakers) and aoûtiens (August holidaymakers), and the big departure weekends bring famous traffic jams. Around 15 August (a public holiday) Paris feels quieter and some small shops close. Then comes la rentrée in early September: children go back to school, people return to work and new projects, clubs and courses start. In Québec, many workers take the construction holiday (les vacances de la construction), traditionally the last two weeks of July.
